calls.title: Summit HVAC — discovery-led call that closes

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Hi Dan, Maya from Relay. Thanks for making time, I know Tuesdays are hectic for dispatch.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Ha, you have no idea. Yeah, happy to chat, I've got about thirty minutes.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Perfect, I'll keep us on track. Before I say anything about Relay, can you walk me through how scheduling works at Summit today, start to finish?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Sure. So we've got eighteen techs across two branches. Every evening our dispatcher, Carla, builds the next day's board in a spreadsheet and texts each tech their route. Then the day starts and everything changes.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: What's the most painful part of that for you?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Same-day changes. A job runs long, a part isn't on the truck, a customer cancels. Carla is on the phone nonstop re-shuffling. Last month we double-booked two techs to the same address twice.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That sounds exhausting for her. When a job runs late, what happens to the customers further down the route?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Honestly, they get a call if Carla remembers. Half the time they don't, and then they call us angry. We've had a couple of one-star reviews that say exactly that.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Roughly how many hours a week would you say Carla spends on the manual re-shuffling and those calls?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Probably three hours a day on the bad days. Call it twelve to fifteen hours a week, and that's on top of her normal work.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: And the double bookings and missed windows, do you have a sense of how many jobs a month you lose or have to redo because of that?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: We tracked it in April. Nine jobs we had to reschedule or eat a discount on. Average ticket is around four hundred dollars, so it adds up.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: So call it three to four thousand a month in slipped revenue plus most of a part-time salary in Carla's hours. Does that sound about right?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Yeah, that's about right. When you say it like that it's worse than I thought.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: What made you take this call now, of all times?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Summer. We go from eighteen to about twenty-four techs with seasonal hires in June, and Carla told me flat out she can't do another summer on the spreadsheet. She'd probably quit.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Got it, so there's a real clock on this. If you had something in place before June, what would good look like for you?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Carla builds the board in ten minutes instead of two hours, techs get updates on their phones automatically, and customers get a text when we're running late so they stop calling us.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That's very close to what Relay does day to day. Let me describe it briefly and then you tell me where it falls short. Relay builds the daily board from your job list and tech skills, re-dispatches automatically when a job runs long, pushes the change to the tech's app, and texts the customer an updated window. Which of those matters most to you?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: The automatic re-dispatch and the customer text. That's the part that's killing us. Does it handle two branches with separate territories?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: It does, each branch gets its own board and dispatcher view, with shared techs if you want. How do you handle techs crossing branches today?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Badly. We try not to. But in summer we have to. Okay, this is interesting. What does something like this cost?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Before I give you a number, can I ask what you're spending today on scheduling, including Carla's time and the dispatch add-on on your current accounting software?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: The add-on is about two hundred a month and we barely use it. Carla's time on this is probably another fifteen hundred a month if I'm honest. We hadn't set a formal budget, but I've got discretion up to about a thousand a month without going to the owner.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That's helpful. For eighteen to twenty-four techs Relay is eleven hundred a month on the annual plan, which includes the customer texting and both branches. So against the roughly five thousand a month you just described in slipped jobs and hours, it pays for itself in the first week of each month.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Eleven hundred. Okay. That's a bit over my line but not by much. The owner, Greg, would need to sign off on anything over a thousand, but he and I decide this kind of thing together and he's aware of the Carla situation.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Good to know. How did the last software purchase like this get approved on your side, what did Greg want to see?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: He wanted to see it actually work with our jobs, not a canned demo. And he wanted a way out if it didn't.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That's fair, and it's how most of our HVAC customers start. We can run a two-week paid pilot on one branch, using your real job list, with a full refund if Carla isn't building the board faster by day ten. Would that give Greg what he needs?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Yeah, that's exactly the kind of thing he'd say yes to. What does the pilot involve on our side?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: About an hour with Carla to import jobs and techs, then she runs her normal day in Relay with me on a shared channel for the first three days. The techs just install the app.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: That's manageable. Carla would love that, honestly. The app part might get some grumbling from the older guys but they'll get over it.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: We see that a lot. Would it help if we did the first tech onboarding in person at your morning huddle?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: That would help a lot, yes.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: So if I've got this right: the main problem is same-day re-dispatch and customer communication, it costs you around five thousand a month today, you need it in place before June when the seasonal techs start, and Greg needs to see it work on real jobs with a way out. Did I miss anything?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: No, that's it exactly. You've listened better than the last two vendors I talked to.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: I appreciate that. Given the June timing, how about we start the pilot the week after next? I can send the pilot agreement tonight, and I'd love fifteen minutes with you and Greg on Thursday to walk through it together.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Thursday works. Greg's usually in by nine. Let's do Thursday at nine thirty.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Booked. And if Greg's comfortable on Thursday, is there anything else that would stop us starting the pilot the following Monday?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: No. Honestly, if Greg's in, let's do it. Send the agreement over and I'll get Carla to block that hour.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Fantastic. I'll send the agreement and a one-page summary of the numbers we discussed within the hour. Thanks Dan, this was a great conversation.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Thanks Maya. Talk Thursday.

calls.title: Bluewater Plumbing — feature dump, unhandled price objection

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Hi Tom, Maya from Relay. Thanks for taking the call.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Hey. Yeah, I've got maybe twenty minutes, I'm between jobs.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: No problem, I'll be quick. So Relay is a field service scheduling and dispatch platform. We help plumbing, HVAC, and electrical companies automate their daily board, route techs efficiently, re-dispatch in real time when jobs run long, and keep customers updated automatically with SMS. We integrate with all the major accounting packages, we've got a mobile app for technicians with GPS tracking, digital job forms, photo capture, and customer signatures, and our routing engine saves customers an average of eleven percent in drive time.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Okay.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: And on top of that, the dispatcher dashboard gives you a live map view of every tech, color-coded by job status, with drag and drop rescheduling. You can set up automated reminders, review requests after each job, and there's a reporting suite with first-time fix rate, revenue per tech, and utilization. A lot of our customers say the reporting alone paid for the product.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Right. How many techs do your customers usually have? We're nine guys.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Nine is a great fit. We have customers from five techs up to several hundred. The platform scales with you, so as you grow you never have to switch systems. And the onboarding is really smooth, we have a dedicated implementation team, video training, and a knowledge base.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: What does it cost?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: For nine techs you'd be on our Growth plan, which is eight hundred and fifty a month on annual billing, and that includes the mobile app, customer texting, and the reporting suite.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Eight fifty a month? That's over ten grand a year. We're a nine-man shop, Maya. That's a lot of money for a calendar.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: I hear you, but it's much more than a calendar. The routing optimization alone typically saves eleven percent in drive time, and the digital forms eliminate paperwork. Plus the review automation drives more Google reviews, which brings in new customers. Most customers see ROI within the first quarter.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Sure, everyone says that. My guys know their routes, they've been driving this town for fifteen years.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That's great local knowledge. What Relay adds on top is the real-time piece: when a job runs long, the system automatically re-sequences the rest of the day and notifies the customers. We also have a parts and inventory module, so techs can see what's on their truck, and a customer portal where clients can book online.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: We looked at DispatchPro last year, they were about half that price.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Yeah, there are a lot of options out there. What sets Relay apart is really the depth of the platform. Let me tell you about our integrations: we sync two-way with your accounting, so invoices flow automatically, and payments can be taken in the field through the app. That closes the loop from dispatch to cash collection.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: What do you mean, closes the loop?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: So the whole lifecycle, from the job being created, through dispatch, execution, invoicing, and payment, all lives in one system of record with full audit trails, and the data model supports multi-entity setups if you ever open a second location.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Uh huh.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: And I should mention our customer success program. Every account gets quarterly business reviews where we go through your utilization and first-time fix metrics and recommend optimizations. Our customers really value that partnership approach.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Look, I don't really have time for quarterly reviews. I'm on the tools half the week myself.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Totally understand, they're optional. The nice thing is the reporting is all self-serve too, so you can check the dashboards whenever you want from your phone. And the setup is really quick, most customers are live within two weeks.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Two weeks of what, though? Who's doing the setup? I don't have an office person.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Our implementation team handles most of it. They'll import your customer list, set up your service types and pricing, configure the mobile app, and train the team. There are a few onboarding calls but it's pretty light. Then you're up and running with the full platform.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Hm. And it's eight fifty regardless? No smaller plan?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Growth is our entry plan for teams over five techs. It really does include everything: dispatch, routing, app, texting, reporting, inventory, portal. The value is in the whole package. And honestly the annual commitment is what lets us offer that price.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Annual. Right.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Yes, twelve months, billed upfront or monthly. Most customers go upfront for the discount. And we have a ninety-day satisfaction window on the enterprise tier, though that tier starts at twenty-five techs.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: So no way out on my plan.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: The annual plan is a commitment, yes, but our retention is over ninety-five percent, so customers are very happy. I'd love to show you the dispatcher dashboard live, it really comes to life when you see the map view with the techs moving around and the drag and drop rescheduling.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Maybe. I'd have to think about it.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Of course. I can also send over some case studies, we have a great one from a plumbing company in Ohio with twelve techs that grew to twenty after switching to Relay, and their first-time fix rate went up fourteen points.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Yeah, just send me some info and I'll take a look when I get a chance.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Absolutely. Would it make sense to put thirty minutes on the calendar next week for a demo, maybe Tuesday or Wednesday?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Let me look at the info first. I'm slammed next week anyway.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Understood. I'll send the case studies, the pricing sheet, and a recorded demo video so you can watch it whenever. And I'll follow up in a couple of weeks.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Sure. Okay, I've got to run, my next job is waiting.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: No problem, thanks Tom, talk soon.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Bye.

calls.title: Ridgeline Electric — rocky start, discovery rescue

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Hi Priya, Maya from Relay. Thanks for the time today.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Hi Maya. I'll be honest, I only took this because our office manager kept forwarding your emails. We have a system already.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Fair enough, I appreciate you being upfront. Let me give you the quick version of Relay then. It's a dispatch and scheduling platform for electrical contractors: automatic daily board, real-time re-dispatch, tech mobile app with job forms, customer SMS updates, and reporting on utilization and first-time fix. It plugs into your accounting so invoices flow through automatically.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: That sounds like what we have. What does it cost?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: For fourteen electricians it's around nine hundred a month on the annual plan.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Nine hundred? We pay three fifty for what we've got. I'm not going to nearly triple our software cost for a nicer-looking calendar. That's a hard no from a budget standpoint.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: I understand. Relay does a lot more than a calendar though, the real-time re-dispatch alone is something most tools in that price range don't do, and the SMS updates dramatically cut inbound calls.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Maybe. Our tool is fine. The guys are used to it.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Okay. Can I take a step back? I've been talking about Relay and I don't actually know anything about how your days go. What does a bad day look like for your dispatcher right now?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: A bad day. Hm. A bad day is when a commercial job runs over and we've got three residential calls stacked behind it. Neha, our coordinator, has to call every one of them, and half the time she can't reach anyone, so a tech shows up to an empty house.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: How often does that happen, a tech arriving to an empty house or a cancelled job they didn't know about?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: More than I'd like. Probably two or three times a week across the team. Each one is a wasted hour plus drive time.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: So call it ten to twelve wasted tech-hours a week. What does a loaded electrician hour cost you, roughly?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: With the truck, about eighty-five dollars. So, what, a thousand a week? I hadn't done that math.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: About four thousand a month in wasted hours, before counting the customers who get annoyed. Does your current tool re-sequence the day automatically when a job runs over, or does Neha do that by hand?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: By hand. It's a scheduling grid, it doesn't know a job is running over until she updates it. Which she can't do while she's on the phone.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That's the gap I'd want to look at with you. What else is on Neha's plate that suffers when she's stuck on those calls?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Quoting. She's supposed to send quotes the same day and they slip to two or three days. We lose some of those to whoever quotes first.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: So there's slipped revenue on quotes too. Roughly how many quotes a month go out late?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Maybe fifteen. We win about a third of quotes normally, less when we're late. Average job is twelve hundred.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Okay. I'm not going to pretend I can attribute all of that to scheduling. But if even two extra quotes a month land because Neha isn't on the phone re-shuffling, that's more than the difference between your current tool and Relay. Is that a fair way to look at it?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: That's a fairer way to look at it than tripling my software bill, yes. Okay. I'm listening.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Thank you. Let me be specific about the one thing that matters here rather than the whole feature list: when a job runs over, Relay re-sequences the remaining jobs for that tech, texts each customer a new window, and only flags Neha if someone replies that the new time doesn't work. Neha goes from making eight calls to handling one exception.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: That would genuinely change her day. Does it work for commercial jobs where the contact is a site foreman rather than a homeowner?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Yes, the contact per job can be anyone, and commercial jobs can be set to notify without offering a reschedule. How do you split commercial versus residential today?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: About sixty-forty commercial. The commercial guys would want the foreman to get the text, not the office. Okay, that works.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Good. Can I ask how a decision like this would get made at Ridgeline? Is it yours, or are there others involved?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: It's mine up to about five hundred a month. Above that I'd bring it to Raj, he's the owner, but he generally goes with my recommendation on operations stuff.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Understood. And is there a timeline you're working to, or is this more of a when-it-makes-sense thing?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Our current contract renews in August, so if we're going to switch, it needs to be decided by July. I don't want to pay for two tools.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: That makes sense, and it gives us time to do this properly. What would you and Raj need to see to be confident this isn't just a nicer calendar?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: I'd want to see it handle a real week of our jobs. Not a demo with fake data. And I'd want Neha's opinion, she's the one living in it.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Then let's do exactly that. We run a two-week pilot on your real job list, with Neha driving it and me on call. It's four hundred for the two weeks, credited against the first year if you go ahead, refunded if Neha says it's not better. Would that work for you?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: That's reasonable. Four hundred is within my authority, so I don't even need Raj for the pilot. When could we start?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: I could have Neha set up next week. How about a forty-five minute kickoff with you and Neha on Monday or Tuesday, and then she runs her normal week in Relay?

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Tuesday afternoon is better, Mondays are chaos. Two o'clock?

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Tuesday at two. I'll send the pilot agreement and a short one-pager with the numbers we worked out, the wasted hours and the quote timing, so you have it for Raj later.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Please do. Put the math in there, that's what he'll care about.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Will do. One last thing: is there anything about the current tool you'd miss? I'd rather know now than find out in week two.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: The invoice sync is the one thing that works well. If that breaks, Neha will hate you.

timeline.speaker: rep
timeline.text: Noted, we'll set up the accounting sync on day one of the pilot so she can compare. Thanks Priya, I appreciate you letting me start over.

timeline.speaker: prospect
timeline.text: Well, the second half was a much better call than the first. See you Tuesday.
